title: Can al-Zaidi separate the sects from the state in Iraq?
gist: The author argues Iran's February 2026 shift from clerical rule to an IRGC generals' juntocracy after Khamenei's assassination has hardened Iraqi Shia militias, doubling the number of factions refusing to disarm from five to ten. Senior Coordination Framework figures told him disarmament depends on the outcome of the US-Iran war rather than on Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's promises to Trump, making his resignation the likely endgame and reframing his real challenge as restoring the state's monopoly over sovereignty from the sects.

themes.theme: Iran's shift from theocracy to juntocracy

insights.claim: The assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on February 28, 2026 and the transfer of the post to his son Mojtaba turned Iran from a theocratic state under the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist into a juntocracy where the final word belongs to generals on the Supreme Council of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
insights.so_what: Iran's decision chain is now military rather than clerical, which shortens escalation timelines and makes regional proxy behavior more operational and less negotiable.
insights.locator: The assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The Iranian regime's ideological hold over followers abroad has not diminished but shifted, taking on a militarized urgency as the Revolutionary Guard tells Shia across the region that if Tehran falls, so does all Shia governance in the region.
insights.so_what: Shared-fate framing recruits Iraqis who never accepted clerical guardianship, widening the mobilization base beyond ideological adherents.
insights.locator: The Iranian regime’s ideological hold over its followers
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Many Iraqis who do not believe in the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist and are not affiliated with armed factions nonetheless accept the argument that threats to Tehran are threats to all Shia.
insights.so_what: Popular buy-in means disarmament efforts face social resistance, not just militia resistance.
insights.locator: Tehran is invoking this shared fate
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The number of armed Iraqi factions refusing to disarm doubled from five to ten after the latest escalation of attacks on Iran and the revelation that the US National Security Council had discussed plans for American ground operations and airstrikes on infrastructure inside Iran.
insights.so_what: US pressure on Iran is directly increasing, not decreasing, the number of armed groups refusing to disarm in Iraq, an inverse response worth modeling.
insights.locator: This belief in a shared existential threat explains
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Harakat al-Nujaba forces threatened to arrest Iraqi army and police forces if they tried to enter the group's headquarters south of Baghdad, inverting the state's monopoly on coercion.
insights.so_what: The state cannot physically enter militia facilities, which makes any disarmament timeline nominal rather than enforceable.
insights.locator: It is also why Harakat al-Nujaba forces threatened
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The United States, coordinating with Saudi Arabia, struck Iraqi militias, and the militias responded by saying they would attack Saudi Arabia within days.
insights.so_what: A direct Iraqi militia strike on Saudi territory is the live escalation vector to watch for Gulf energy and shipping risk.
insights.locator: In this context, the United States, in coordination with Saudi Arabia
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: Iraq as a state of sects, not institutions

insights.claim: Despite a 2005 constitution stipulating a parliamentary system, Iraqi state institutions from top to bottom have been divided along sectarian lines and have become the property of the sects rather than of the state.
insights.so_what: Any reform read as institutional will fail unless it changes the sectarian allocation, the actual operating system of Iraqi governance.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Iraq is neither a state of individual rule nor institutional rule and neither parliamentary nor presidential, but a state of sectarian rule in which each sect holds a political institution, a presidential-level post, and an agreed sovereign ministry.
insights.so_what: Use sect allocation, not formal constitutional labels, to predict who controls oil, finance, and security decisions in Baghdad.
insights.locator: It is, simply, a state of sectarian rule
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Except for the Kurds, Iraq's sects have consolidated into two political institutions: the Coordination Framework founded in 2021 as an alliance of all Shia parties bar the Sadrists, and the National Political Council representing the Sunnis.
insights.so_what: Two bodies, not the cabinet, are the real counterparties for anyone assessing Iraqi policy continuity.
insights.locator: Except for the Kurds, the sects have coalesced
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: The Coordination Framework sits above the state

insights.claim: After the Sadrists won the 2021 elections and tried to build a cross-sectarian tripartite alliance with Sunnis and Kurds, the Iran-backed Coordination Framework confronted them politically and with force, compelled Muqtada al-Sadr to withdraw, and monopolized Shia political decisionmaking.
insights.so_what: The precedent shows cross-sectarian governments get broken by force, setting the ceiling on what any reformist prime minister can attempt.
insights.locator: After winning the 2021 elections, the Sadrists
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Former Prime Minister Mohammed al-Sudani won the 2025 elections with a mixed Shia-Sunni bloc after distancing himself from the Coordination Framework, then pragmatically returned to it rather than challenge it over government formation.
insights.so_what: Electoral victory does not translate into governing independence in Iraq; even winners must re-enter the sectarian bloc.
insights.locator: Former Prime Minister Mohammed al-Sudani clearly understood
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Since 2025 the Coordination Framework has established itself as a structural mechanism above the state, imposing its will in parliament and appointing both the president of the republic and the speaker of parliament.
insights.so_what: Control of the presidency and speakership means the Framework can block or unwind any US-backed agenda regardless of who holds the premiership.
insights.locator: Since 2025, the Coordination Framework has succeeded
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: Washington's bet on al-Zaidi and its likely failure

insights.claim: The United States tried to break Iraq's sectarian structure by backing a prime minister from outside the Coordination Framework, threatening to cut off support if Baghdad chose a Tehran-aligned candidate and hosting new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the White House.
insights.so_what: US Iraq policy is now personalized around one prime minister, making the relationship fragile to his political survival.
insights.locator: This year, the United States attempted to break this sectarian structure
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The US administration wants al-Zaidi to fully disarm Iraqi armed factions ahead of an American troop withdrawal from Iraq by the end of September.
insights.so_what: A hard September withdrawal date attached to an unachievable disarmament precondition is a scheduled policy collision.
insights.locator: The US administration hopes that al-Zaidi
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Senior Coordination Framework members told the author that disarming Iraqi armed factions is tied to the outcome of the ongoing US-Iranian war, and that important Framework forces will not back al-Zaidi unless the Iranian regime's survival is assured or Tehran consents.
insights.so_what: Disarmament is a function of the Iran war outcome, not of Iraqi domestic politics, so no Baghdad-level deal can deliver it.
insights.locator: Instead, senior members of the Coordination Framework told the author
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Al-Zaidi has said in Framework meetings he would risk armed confrontation to disarm the factions, but knows the Framework will not permit a Shia-Shia military confrontation, leaving resignation as his only option once the White House withdraws support for failing the mission.
insights.so_what: The base case is al-Zaidi's resignation and renewed Iraqi political instability before year-end, a risk to Iraqi oil governance and US-Iraq contracts.
insights.locator: Although al-Zaidi stated in one of the Framework’s meetings
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Experience with all previous Iraqi prime ministers shows that neither decisions nor external support matter most; what matters is an agreed agenda among all parties on core issues such as disarming militias.
insights.so_what: Discount White House visits and signed economic agreements as predictors of Iraqi policy delivery; look instead for cross-party consensus.
insights.locator: Despite the clamorous atmosphere and dazzling spotlight
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Unless al-Zaidi curbs the role of sectarian institutions in shaping state decisions, he will be another implementer of policies decided by sectarian councils, and his real battle is restoring the state's monopoly over its own sovereignty rather than disarming factions.
insights.so_what: Reframes the benchmark for judging Iraqi reform: sovereignty over sectarian councils, not militia headcount.
insights.locator: The battle before al-Zaidi, then, is not disarming the factions
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
